articles.title: After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly | Jamie Oliver
articles.summary: This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful! More than 20 years ago, when I started the campaign and TV series School Dinners, I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our…
body: Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, but twice the recommended sugar, school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.

But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’s social connection and sense of belonging. Well-fed kids are happier, have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, and their learning and behaviour improve, too.
It’s no surprise that 80% of teachers agree that unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: could the new dog’s tricks make her into a star?
articles.summary: Two women I meet on our walk are way more interested in Jean than me – and insist she’ll clean up if we enter her in the local dog show. It’s a Saturday morning and I’m walking the dog on a vast bit of scrubland. The path in front of me is parched and deserted.
body: Only when I turn the corner myself do I see that everything is fine: the dog is dashing from one woman to the other, tail wagging, and the women are both delighted. Meanwhile, their own dogs stand to one side, staring balefully at the ground, leads trailing.
“Let me give you one of these,” says the first woman, handing me a bit of paper from a stack. It’s advertising a dog show, taking place on the same scrubland the next afternoon.
“We’ve got a celebrity compere,” says the first, mentioning a name I’ve never heard.
“Anyway, you can register online, and Jean would be most welcome,” says the second woman.

articles.title: ‘We’ve been on a good run lately. We’ve not had a row for weeks!’: Coleen and Wayne Rooney on marriage, mistakes and making reality TV
articles.summary: His on-pitch triumphs (and off-pitch scandals), her turn as Wagatha Christie … for years, the football power couple have made headlines, despite efforts to keep their lives private. So why are they now about to reveal all on screen?
body: “If you’d said to me 10 years ago, ‘You’re going to be doing a TV show about the family’, I would have said, ‘No chance’,” Wayne Rooney says. Few would have disagreed. After all, he and his wife Coleen had spent their adult lifetime running away from the public gaze. And not very successfully, at that.

Wayne, a wonderful footballer with the strength of a bull and agility of an acrobat, was often back-page news. He scored 253 goals for Manchester United (overtaking Bobby Charlton’s record), 53 for England (the record until Harry Kane surpassed him in 2023), is still England’s youngest goal scorer (17 years and 317 days), won five Premier League titles, was twice young player of the year and was voted player of the year by both his peers and football journalists in 2009/10.

But it’s the front pages that have caused him the bother. His off-pitch scandals have been even more newsworthy than his on-pitch triumphs. As with his football, he showed a precocious talent for hogging the headlines with stories about drunkenness and debauchery.
points: So why are they now about to reveal all on screen?

articles.title: John Wilson Is Still Shocked That ‘The History of Concrete’ Got Made
articles.summary: Wilson’s discursive new film is out now from Magnolia Pictures.
body: While filmmaker John Wilson was touring his latest movie, The History of Concrete, around Europe, he was gifted a large slab of the material.

“I had to fly from Barcelona to Warsaw with a ton of concrete in my bag that I thought was basically contraband because it was sidewalk tiles that people literally ripped out of the ground [in Barcelona] to give to me,” he tells Vogue over Zoom. “Thankfully, they didn’t weigh my bag at all on the Polish airline.”
So why concrete, and why a feature-length film (Wilson’s first) about it? It’s a long story. “I accidentally made a movie, in certain ways,” Wilson says.

When the foundation of his house begins to crack and the basement floods, Wilson becomes fascinated with the ubiquity of concrete in our modern lives. “It’s embarrassing to know so little about something that occupies so much of your visual environment,” he narrates while the camera pans into a freshly paved sidewalk. Thus begins an odyssey that will take Wilson to Rome, Astoria, a 3,100-mile race in Queens, a Las Vegas concrete convention, a rock concert, and back, all in the effort to secure funding to make a movie about concrete, guided by the principles of the Hallmark class.
points: Wilson’s discursive new film is out now from Magnolia Pictures.

articles.title: “London Is About Being Free”—Seán McGirr on Tomorrow’s Homecoming for McQueen
articles.summary: Three years after his arrival, McGirr’s McQueen show will be the brand’s first on the London Fashion Week schedule since February 2001.
body: “In a brand with the legacy of McQueen, it takes a while to learn the codes. In each collection so far, I’ve done something slightly different in order to understand certain periods of his work. Now, with this one, I want to go to the next level.”

Seán McGirr is in the midst of fittings at the McQueen studio in Clerkenwell, preparing for tomorrow night. That is when he will make his pitch at transcending the sum total of all things McQueen absorbed during his nearly three years at the house.

However tomorrow’s return means a great deal both to London Fashion Week—which is perennially dedicated to cheerleading the British capital as a key crucible of creativity—as well as to McQueen and McGirr. “It felt like the right moment, and everything aligned,” says the designer, adding: “London is about being free.”

This collection will reconnect McGirr with some of those formative London influences while also bringing McQueen back into the orbit of some of its first-generation collaborators. One of them is the jeweler and sculptor Shaun Leane, one of Alexander McQueen’s closest creative collaborators, who has created three new pieces for tomorrow’s show.
points: Three years after his arrival, McGirr’s McQueen show will be the brand’s first on the London Fashion Week schedule since February 2001.

articles.title: Sweet and Tangy Collard Greens
articles.summary: Bacon, cider vinegar, and a little sugar give these tender collard greens their savory, sweet-tangy flavor.
body: Collard greens have deep roots in Southern cooking. They’re a fixture on New Year’s Day, when eating greens is said to bring prosperity in the year ahead. Chef Julia Sullivan of Henrietta Red in Nashville serves them alongside black-eyed peas every January 1. “It’s something my mom has always done, and I think my grandparents, too,” she says. “It’s a superstitious thing.”

Sullivan’s collard greens get their savory, subtly smoky flavor from bacon, onion, garlic, and red pepper flakes. They simmer until silky-tender in just under an hour, then get a sweet-tart finish from apple cider vinegar and a little sugar. This recipe intentionally leans tangy. If you like your collard greens less acidic, start with 2 Tbsp. vinegar instead of the full ¼ cup, then add more to taste.
points: Bacon, cider vinegar, and a little sugar give these tender collard greens their savory, sweet-tangy flavor.

articles.title: Onigiri (Japanese Rice Balls)
articles.summary: Three savory fillings, one simple technique, and no special equipment required.
body: Stuffed with savory fillings and wrapped in crisp nori, Japanese rice balls called onigiri are made for eating on the go. A convenience-store staple in Japan, they’re just as handy tucked into a lunch box or picnic basket.

The key to onigiri that hold their shape is properly cooked Japanese short-grain rice. Rinsing and soaking the rice helps it cook evenly; shaping it while still slightly warm helps the grains stick together. Use damp, salted hands to prevent sticking—no rice cooker or onigiri mold required.

This version offers three fillings: creamy tuna mayo, tart and salty umeboshi (pickled plums), or spicy kimchi. Once you’ve got the technique down, feel free to experiment with cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat. Just avoid anything too wet, which can make the rice balls difficult to shape.

Japanese short-grain rice, often labeled sushi rice at US supermarkets, is the best choice. When cooked, the grains cling together enough for the onigiri to hold their shape. Long-grain rice, such as jasmine or basmati, won’t hold together as well.
points: Three savory fillings, one simple technique, and no special equipment required.

articles.title: 12 Friendsgiving-Friendly Airbnbs to Book If You Want to Be the Martha Stewart of Your Group
articles.summary: Equipped with multiple bedrooms, full kitchens, and grand dining tables, these rentals will help you and your crew celebrate America’s favorite holiday in style.
body: Thanksgiving has taken many forms since its inception in 1621, and if there’s anything the modern portmanteau “Friendsgiving” has taught us, it’s that you don’t need a traditional family to enjoy America’s favorite feast. And I’m here to tell you you don’t need to have the perfect home to host one, either. Thanks to Airbnb, you can simply rent your dream holiday house.

For all you East Coasters, there’s an abundance of country-chic properties nestled in nature just waiting to help foster quality time without the stress—you know, the kinds of sprawling homesteads Martha Stewart would be thrilled to baste a turkey in. The Airbnbs on this list are ideal for a group getaway, equipped with multiple bedrooms, full kitchens (with ovens big enough for your bird), and grand dining tables, so you can whip up Thanksgiving dinner with ease. Some even have game rooms and saunas, perfect for winding down after the big meal.
From lakeside log cabins in New Hampshire to restored farmhouses in the Hudson Valley, these are the best Friendsgiving-friendly Airbnbs on the East Coast, separated by state.

articles.title: Cottage Cheese Lasagna
articles.summary: Love cottage cheese? You’ll love this lasagna. Hate cottage cheese? You’ll still love this lasagna.
body: Cottage cheese lasagna skeptics, hear us out. Unlike ricotta, which can turn chalky, small-curd, whole-milk cottage cheese stays moist through the long bake. And when mixed with nutty Parmesan, melty Fontina, eggs, and garlic, it makes an exceptionally creamy lasagna filling.
This may not be nonna’s classic (we’ve got BA’s Best Lasagna for that), but it’s deeply savory, exceptionally cheesy, and considerably easier to assemble.
Whole-milk cottage cheese is nonnegotiable. Lighter versions can make the lasagna watery and less flavorful. We prefer small-curd for texture, but large-curd works just fine if that’s what you have.

Regular dried lasagna noodles go directly into the baking dish—no boiling or soaking required. The relatively loose tomato sauce provides enough moisture to cook the noodles until al dente as the lasagna bakes.

articles.title: CFDA CEO Steven Kolb Has Resigned Following Altercation with Peta
articles.summary: Kolb, who was seen on video physically restraining protestors at a Cos show on Sunday, was previously placed on leave.
body: Steven Kolb is stepping down from his role as CEO of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), the organization announced on Friday night.

“Steven Kolb has been a dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion throughout his more than two decades at the CFDA, including 15 years as CEO,” the CFDA Board said in a statement. “We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry. He leaves the organization well positioned, with a clear mission and dedicated team, to carry out the important work ahead as we look to the future of American fashion.”

“After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” Kolb said in a statement. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organization to begin a new chapter.”

articles.title: Parker House Rolls
articles.summary: These classic American dinner rolls have buttery golden tops and a signature folded shape.
body: With burnished tops, buttery layers, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt, Parker House rolls are the classic American dinner roll. Created at Boston’s Parker House Hotel in the 19th century, the soft, fluffy yeast rolls are sometimes called pocketbook rolls due to their signature folded shape. Serve them alongside Thanksgiving turkey or holiday ham, then pry open any leftovers to slather with honey or jam for breakfast.

Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, this Parker House roll recipe is straightforward enough for novice bread bakers: The dough is easy to knead by hand (though a stand mixer works too). Brushing each piece with melted butter before folding creates the rolls’ characteristic shape, while a second swab after baking gives them their sheen.
What makes a Parker House roll different from a regular dinner roll?

It’s all in the fold. Instead of shaping the dough into balls, Parker House rolls are shaped into rectangles, brushed with butter, and folded over themselves. The result is their distinctive pocketbook shape and a buttery seam that makes them easy to pull apart.
